title: Hegel and the Challenge of Spinoza
subtitle: A Study in German Idealism, 1801–1831
abstract: In an earlier study (Cambridge 2005) I documented the discussion regarding the nature of humankind that preoccupied the German intelligentsia in the second half of the eighteenth century. Jacobi intervened in the discussion bringing Spinoza to the scene, with results that affected the reception of Kant’s Critique of Reason. In the present study I pursue the same theme, but in the completely different conceptual and social context of early Romanticism. Humankind’s vocation assumes rather the form of God’s vocation. I explore this change with reference to the three canonical post-Kantians, Fichte, Schelling and Hegel, with Jacobi occasionally interloping, all in their post-1800 phase, taking the date of Hegel’s death (1831) as my occasionally moving end-post. How to save subjectivity in the face of Spinoza’s monism was still the challenge. I argue that Hegel met this challenge, not by disproving monism, which was also the assumption behind classical metaphysics, but by simply rendering it moot. In this, Hegel was much closer in spirit to Kant and Fichte than to Schelling. I consider this work a philosophical argument in historical medium.

title: The Science of Logic
subtitle: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
role: Translation, with notes and introductory study
abstract: A complete translation of Hegel’s Wissenschaft der Logik — the 'Greater Logic' — with translator’s notes and an introductory study. Corrections to the translation are collected in the Notes on the Translation.

title: Freedom and Religion in Kant and His Immediate Successors
subtitle: The Vocation of Humankind, 1774–1800
abstract: A study of the debate over the vocation of humankind that preoccupied the German intelligentsia in the second half of the eighteenth century, and of how Jacobi’s introduction of Spinoza into that debate shaped the reception of Kant’s critical philosophy.
